text: Jack Dorsey began developing the early idea for Twitter in 2006 while working at the podcasting company Odeo. The concept originated during a "daylong brainstorming session" where Dorsey, then an undergraduate student, proposed using an SMS service to communicate with a small group. The original project code name was twttr, inspired by Flickr and the five-character length of American SMS short codes, with Evan Williams later attributing the name to Noah Glass. The domain twitter.com was already in use, so the team purchased it six months after launching twttr and renamed the service Twitter. The developers initially considered "10958" as the SMS short code but changed it to "40404" for ease of use and memorability. Work on the project began in February 2006, and Dorsey published the first Twitter post, "just setting up my twttr," in March 2006. The first prototype, developed by Dorsey and contractor Florian Weber, was used internally at Odeo, with the full version launched publicly on July 15, 2006. In October 2006, Biz Stone, Evan Williams, Dorsey, and others formed Obvious Corporation and acquired Odeo, including its assets. Williams fired Noah Glass, who remained silent about his role until 2011. Twitter spun off into its own company in April 2007. The service was initially ambiguous in definition, described as a social network or microblogging platform, but evolved into being primarily an information network. The term "tweet" emerged from a search by Craig Hockenberry for a shorter way to refer to posting a Twitter update, later adopted by Blaine Cook. The hashtag was introduced in 2007 by Chris Messina, inspired by Internet Relay Chat and Jaiku, and was eventually adopted by Twitter despite mixed initial reactions. Twitter's popularity surged at the 2007 South by Southwest Interactive (SXSWi) conference, where usage increased from 20,000 to 60,000 tweets per day, and the service won the festival's Web Award with the remark "we'd like to thank you in 140 characters or less. And we just did!" Elon Musk joined as a user in 2009. Twitter won the "Breakout of the Year" Webby Award in 2009 and was named Word of the Year by the Global Language Monitor that same year. By February 2010, users were sending 50 million tweets per day, and by March 2010, over 70,000 applications were registered. In June 2010, about 65 million tweets were posted daily, equating to roughly 750 tweets per second, increasing to about 140 million daily by March 2011. Twitter moved to third place among social networking sites by January 2009. The platform saw usage spikes during major events, such as the 2010 FIFA World Cup, where 2,940 tweets per second were posted after Japan scored against Cameroon, followed by 3,085 after the Lakers' NBA Finals victory and 3,283 after Japan's win over Denmark. A record of 7,196 tweets per second was set during the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup Final. When Michael Jackson died on June 25, 2009, Twitter servers crashed due to 100,000 tweets per hour containing "Michael Jackson." The highest recorded rate, 143,199 tweets per second, occurred in Japan during a screening of the movie Castle in the Sky on August 3, 2013. In June 2009, Tony La Russa sued Twitter for trade infringement after an impersonation of him, leading to a settlement and the introduction of Verified Accounts. Ashton Kutcher's account became the first with a million followers in 2009. Twitter played a major role in the 2009 Iranian presidential election protests. On January 22, 2010, NASA astronaut T. J. Creamer posted the first unassisted off-Earth Twitter message from the International Space Station. By late November 2010, an average of a dozen updates per day were posted on the astronauts' communal account, @NASA_Astronauts. Twitter acquired Atebits on April 11, 2010, which developed the Apple Design Award-winning Twitter client Tweetie, becoming the official client for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. The Library of Congress began archiving all tweets from 2006 onward, initially archiving all new tweets, though it switched to selective archiving in 2018. From September to October 2010, Twitter rolled out "New Twitter," allowing users to view pictures and videos directly within the platform and introducing a redesigned interface with '@mentions' and 'Retweets' above the stream and 'Messages' and 'Log Out' in a top black bar. The "New Twitter" experience was fully rolled out by November 1, 2010. In April 2011, Twitter tested a new homepage and phased out the "Old Twitter," though a glitch delayed the transition, with the retro homepage remaining until April 20. On December 8, 2011, Twitter introduced the "Fly" design, adding Connect and Discover tabs, a redesigned profile, and timeline, with a layout similar to Facebook. In February 2012, Twitter announced a partnership with Yandex, a Russian search engine, to leverage real-time news feeds. On March 21, 2012, Twitter celebrated its sixth birthday with 140 million users and 340 million tweets per day. In April 2012, Twitter opened an office in Detroit and expanded its Dublin office. In March 2011, a cobra escaped from the Bronx Zoo, leading to the creation of a parody account @BronxZoosCobra, which gained widespread attention. On June 5, 2012, Twitter unveiled a modified logo removing text to feature a redesigned bird. By December 18, 2012, monthly active users had increased by 42% and surpassed 200 million. Pope Benedict XVI joined Twitter on December 18, 2012, using the handle @pontifex, which answers questions via the hashtag #askpontifex. In 2012, "tweet" was added to the Oxford English Dictionary. Vine, a short video service, was launched in 2013. On January 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Crashlytics to expand its mobile developer products. On April 18, 2013, Twitter launched a music app called Twitter Music for iPhone. On August 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Trendrr, followed by MoPub on September 9, 2013. As of September 2013, 200 million users sent over 400 million tweets daily, with nearly 60% from mobile devices. In April 2013, the Syrian Electronic Army hacked the Associated Press account, causing a significant short-term market impact, and later hacked Barack Obama's account. During Super Bowl XLVII on February 3, 2013, Kraft Foods VP Lisa Mann tweeted "You can still dunk in the dark" after a power outage, a moment that became a milestone in daily cultural commentary. Twitter went public in 2013 through an IPO that raised $1.8 billion. 2014 was a difficult year for the company, with market pessimism. In April 2014, Twitter redesigned its site to resemble Facebook, featuring profile pictures and biographies on the left and a full-width header with parallax scrolling, which remained the main desktop layout until July 2019. Growth slowed in 2015. In September 2016, Twitter shares rose 20% after reports of takeover interest, with potential buyers including Alphabet, Microsoft, Salesforce, Verizon, and The Walt Disney Company. The board was open to a deal by the end of 2016, but no acquisition occurred due to concerns over abuse and harassment. In 2017, Elon Musk first expressed interest in acquiring Twitter. In June 2017, Twitter revamped its dashboard to improve the user experience. Vine was shut down in 2017. On April 29, 2018, Solstar sent the first commercial tweet from space using commercial infrastructure during a New Shepard flight. In May 2018, Twitter introduced an algorithm to hide replies deemed detractive, requiring users to click "Show more replies" to view them. From 2015 to 2018, Twitter suspended over a million accounts related to terrorism. In 2018, the tweet length limit was increased from 140 to 280 characters, after a trial in 2017. In 2019, Twitter released another user interface redesign. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Twitter experienced significant growth but also faced challenges with misinformation. The platform began marking tweets with misleading information and adding fact-check links, though it sometimes incorrectly flagged factual content as misleading. In May 2020, two tweets from U.S. President Donald Trump were marked as "potentially misleading" and linked to fact-checks. Trump responded by signing an executive order to weaken Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. After the January 6 United States Capitol attack, Twitter banned Trump, citing violation of its "glorification of violence" policy, drawing criticism from American conservatives and European leaders. In 2020, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian pushed pandemic conspiracy theories on Twitter, which is blocked in mainland China but used as a public diplomacy tool by Chinese officials. China's ambassador to South Africa also made these claims on Twitter. In May 2020, Twitter placed fact-check labels on two of these tweets.

In May 2020, Twitter moderators marked two tweets from U.S. President Donald Trump as "potentially misleading" and linked to a fact-check. Trump responded by signing an executive order to weaken Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which limits social media sites' liability for content moderation decisions. After the January 6 United States Capitol attack, Twitter banned Trump, claiming he violated "the glorification of violence policy." The ban drew criticism from American conservatives and European leaders, who viewed it as an interference with freedom of speech. In 2020, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian promoted conspiracy theories about the pandemic on Twitter, a platform blocked in mainland China but used by Chinese officials for public diplomacy. China's ambassador to South Africa also made these claims on Twitter. In May 2020, Twitter placed fact-check labels on two Chinese government tweets that falsely suggested the virus originated in the U.S. and was brought to China by Americans. In January 2021, Hua Chunying renewed the conspiracy theory that the SARS-CoV-2 virus originated in the United States from the U.S. military biology laboratory Fort Detrick, continuing to reference it on Twitter and urging the U.S. government to open Fort Detrick for investigation. In April 2021, Twitter announced the establishment of its African headquarters in Ghana. On June 5, 2021, the Nigerian government issued an indefinite ban on Twitter, citing "misinformation and fake news spread through it have had real world violent consequences," following the platform's removal of tweets by Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari. The ban was criticized by Amnesty International. In 2021, Twitter began the research phase of Bluesky, an open-source decentralized social media protocol allowing users to choose their preferred algorithmic curation. The same year, Twitter launched Twitter Spaces, a social audio feature; "super follows," a subscription model for exclusive content; and a beta of "ticketed Spaces," which makes access to certain audio rooms paid. Twitter unveiled a redesign in August 2021, featuring adjusted colors and a new Chirp font that improves left-alignment for most Western languages. In June 2022, Twitter announced a partnership with e-commerce giant Shopify to launch a sales channel app for U.S. Shopify merchants. On August 23, 2022, the contents of a whistleblower complaint by former information security head Peiter Zatko to the U.S. Congress were published. Zatko had been fired by Twitter in January 2022; the complaint alleges Twitter failed to disclose data breaches, had negligent security, violated U.S. securities regulations, and breached a prior settlement with the Federal Trade Commission over user data protection, and claims the Indian government forced Twitter to hire an agent to gain direct access to user data. Elon Musk initiated an acquisition of Twitter, Inc. on April 14, 2022, and concluded it on October 27, 2022. Musk began buying shares in January 2022, becoming the company's largest shareholder by April with a 9.1 percent ownership stake. Twitter invited Musk to join its board, an offer he initially accepted before declining. On April 14, Musk made an unsolicited offer to purchase the company, to which Twitter's board responded with a "poison pill" strategy before unanimously accepting Musk's $44 billion buyout offer on April 25. Musk stated he planned to introduce new features, make algorithms open-source, combat spambot accounts, and promote free speech, framing the acquisition as the cornerstone of X, an "everything app." In July, Musk announced he would terminate the agreement, claiming Twitter breached the agreement by refusing to crack down on spambot accounts. The company filed a lawsuit in the Delaware Court of Chancery, with a trial scheduled for the week of October 17. Weeks before the trial began, Musk reversed course and announced he would proceed with the acquisition. The deal closed on October 28, with Musk becoming the new owner and CEO of Twitter. The company was taken private and merged into a new parent company named X Corp. Musk fired several top executives, including former CEO Parag Agrawal. Musk proposed reforms and laid off half of the company's workforce. Hundreds of employees resigned after Musk issued an ultimatum demanding they commit to "extremely hardcore" work. Linda Yaccarino was appointed CEO of X Corp. In July 2023, the Twitter service was rebranded as X. Reactions to the buyout were mixed, with praise for Musk's planned reforms and vision, especially his emphasis on free speech, but criticism over fears of increased misinformation, disinformation, harassment, and hate speech. In the United States, conservatives largely supported the acquisition, while many liberals and former employees expressed concerns about Musk's intentions. Since becoming owner, Musk faced backlash for handling the company and account suspensions, including the December 2022 suspensions of ten journalists. Elon Musk completed his acquisition of Twitter in October 2022; Musk served as CEO until June 2023 when he was succeeded by Linda Yaccarino. The Twitter service was rebranded to X on July 23, 2023, and its domain name changed from twitter.com to x.com on May 17, 2024. Yaccarino resigned on July 9, 2025. Now operating as X, the platform closely resembles its predecessor but includes additional features such as long-form texts, account monetization options, audio-video calls, integration with xAI's Grok chatbot, job search, and a repurposing of the verification system as a subscription premium. Several legacy features were removed after Musk's acquisition, including Circles, NFT profile pictures, and the experimental pronouns in profiles feature. Musk's goals included transforming X into a "digital town square" and an "everything app" similar to WeChat. X has faced significant controversy post-rebranding, including the release of the Twitter Files, suspensions of ten journalists' accounts, labeling media outlets as "state-affiliated," and restricting their visibility. Criticism has also arisen over viral misinformation, hate speech (especially antisemitism), and child pornography. In response to allegations it deemed unfair, X Corp. has pursued legal action against nonprofit organizations Media Matters and the Center for Countering Digital Hate.
